---
title: "A surprising riposte"
author:
  - brian-dillon
date: "2026-11-30"
categories: [psycholinguistics, surprisal]
description: "On using many language models to test Surprisal theory, in reply to a recent critique."
---

It’s been an interesting couple of years for the Surprisal theory of human sentence processing, which has enjoyed an unusually long run as a leading candidate for a (mostly) unifying theory of sentence processing[^1]. 

Surprisal theory is maybe a bit of a misnomer; the idea that surprisal is a key information theoretic correlate of syntactic processing has been grounded in several distinct process models[^2]. But let’s make things concrete, and zoom in on some key tenets of just one influential capital-S *Surprisal* theory[^3], Levy's (2008) proposal. They are:

- Sentence comprehension is a process of inference over latent structures: trees, dependency parses, or maybe something fancier.   
- Comprehenders maintain a probability distribution over a (very) large number of such latent structures as candidate hypotheses of the input.  
- With each new linguistic unit that comes in, the comprehender gets new evidence to update this probability distribution with.   
- Under certain assumptions, the surprisal (negative log probability) of the next linguistic unit corresponds to the KL divergence between the probability distribution over latent structures before and after seeing the relevant unit; that KL divergence captures the key notion of ‘belief update’ that’s at the heart of the theory.   
- Hence, lower-case-s *surprisal* is the primary index of the key process that underlies human sentence comprehension, and we thus predict to see pervasive effects of surprisal in word-by-word processing difficulty.

This is a great idea[^4]. It is a simple theory rooted in a straightforward (though contestable) computational-level characterization of what sentence processing is all about \- it’s just “find the sentence”[^5]. There’s also ample evidence that people are broadly sensitive to *predictability* in online processing*,* as operationalized with (e.g.) Cloze probability — so Surprisal theory would seem to have both conceptual and empirical wind in its sails. This idea, however, seems to have become decoupled from the workaday practice of some psycholinguists, especially in and around the computational corners of our field. 

A very common analysis is to use some language model to operationalize lower-case-s surprisal, derive a metric for each word/linguistic unit in a corpus, and see if that measurement correlates with processing difficulty. There’s enormous evidence it does, and a major achievement of this line of research is showing that this effect obtains over many orders of magnitude of underlying probability. For example, Smith & Levy, 2013 showed this with a low order *n*\-gram language model. Although an *n–*gram model isn’t Surprisal, the theory, this is still a real improvement over the Cloze probability approach to investigating the effect of word predictability, since Cloze typically can’t yield reliable enough estimates of the relevant conditional probabilities at the tail end of the distribution. Thus language models of different stripes became useful practical tools that are deployed tactically to overcome a key challenge, serving as a microscope that lets us ask what happens when the numbers get very small. 

But the adoption of these tools has come at a cost: it has led to a gradual bifurcation of surprisal practice from Surprisal theory, because the language models that yield the relevant surprisal estimates mostly don’t correspond to the underlying Surprisal theory expressed above at all: a trigram model doesn’t implement Surprisal theory. Imperceptably over time, it seems the microscope has become the theory — weird analogy, but it seems to me that this is basically what has happened\!

A pair of recent papers shine a light on this unhappy state of affairs. Cotterell (2026) makes the straightforward point that a language model is a probability distribution over the next token in context, and we’re free to construct any probability distribution (ergo any language model) we like if we do not have any substantive constraints placed on this process. So it is of course possible to construct a language model that predicts all human processing difficulty word by word, and in this sense, lower-case-s surprisal theory[^6] is without any content; it just amounts to saying that there is an ordering of difficulty over linguistic units in their contexts that can be projected onto a language model. This is, in other words, a redescription of the data. To upgrade surprisal theory to Surprisal theory, we need “rational grounding:” a commitment to some computational or algorithmic level characterization of the process that must be met by candidate language models. Makes total sense to me, and I think most psycholinguists would consider this a starting premise of the enterprise. 

Buxo-Lugo et al (2026) take it one step further, and argue that the rot is more widespread than might be apparent. One key point they make is that a language model is an implicit commitment to a process model, since different models engage different representations and processes to deliver their surprisal estimates. And this is true even within language models of a single computational class: GPT-2 and Pythia may look like the same kind of autoregressive transformer architecture, but Buxo-Lugo and colleagues show that they take very different paths across their hidden layers to compute next word surprisal. Presumably, this means they implement very different process models, maybe even corresponding to different psycholinguistic theories. When we don’t really understand this process, as is the case with transformer models, then the resulting surprisal values become uninterpretable on their own. And because these models display different algorithmic and process level commitments, the surprisal values they deliver are incommensurate and cannot be treated as interchangeable estimates of surprisal. Importantly, their argument holds even if you have two models that you might think realize the same basic “theory” of language processing, like GPT-2 and Pythia.

Buxo-Lugo and colleagues note that work from our own group provides an example of this deleterious practice: *“It is now common to see research articles compute surprisal measure from dozens to hundreds of language models and, assuming that they are interchangeable, use them to study whether a word’s predictability in context reflects processing diﬀiculty (Shain et al., 2024; **Timkey et al., 2026**; Wilcox et al., 2020, 2021).* (Buxo-Lugo et al., 2026; p. 3\)*”*  This was notable to me, because I agree entirely with Buxo-Lugo et al. that the surprisal from a single language model implies the process-level commitments inherent in the model, and probably isn’t all that interpretable in isolation. But I did not find this at odds with the practice of using hundreds of language models to compute surprisal and comparing them against the human data to test Surprisal theory as we have pursued in our work. Why not? 

In short: despite Buxo-Lugo et al’s well-taken critique, I still think there’s usefulness in a utilitarian framing of the language models’ surprisal as ‘a useful way to approximate a value of interest that is critical for our theory.’ If we would like to very seriously test Surprisal theory, then we *need* to have some defensible estimate of the human-level subjective probability estimates that Surprisal theory places at the heart of the theorized syntactic belief update process, otherwise the theory can’t really be tested in any meaningful way. And I don’t think we have a better option on hand at the moment. 

Now, if you came to me with the output of a single language model – GPT-2, say — and showed me that it couldn’t capture the cost of syntactic disambiguation, I might not be all that moved. There’s too many ways for a single model to fail, and I would agree with Buxo-Lugo and colleagues that there’s too much implicit process baked into GPT-2 for it to stand as the sole avatar of the “true human surprisal” values that would provide a meaningful test of Surprisal theory. I’d probably feel that way if you showed me comparable results from 3, 4, 10 models.   
    
But if you showed me this was true for more than 400 different models (like Will Timkey did in our recent paper), then I find this much more compelling (though admittedly not airtight) as a test of Surprisal theory. This seems like a sensible reaction if you regard an individual language model’s surprisal estimate as *interpretable* but *highly unreliable,* rather than *uninterpretable* and *incommensurate* with other black-box models’ surprisal. The specific interpretation of *interpretable* I have in mind here is ‘an estimator of the probability distribution of interest’ \- from this perspective, using a language model’s surprisal estimates is not fundamentally different than using any sample statistic to infer a latent parameter of interest. But of course, we have no guarantees that the language model surprisal is a *good* estimator of the human subjective probability distribution we wish to approximate. I don’t think it’s wise to assume it is \- and it’s in this sense that I think they are *highly unreliable*. To extend the statistical estimator analogy, I think it’s probably wise to assume that each model’s surprisal estimates have very high error, such that we should expect on average any individual model’s estimates to be off quite a bit from the actual probability distribution we wish to approximate. But that doesn’t mean it’s not a useful estimator.

If this analogy holds, then any claims based on a single language model approximating human language performance should be taken with a massive grain of salt \- we just have no clue whether the estimated surprisal values are in any way close to the target parameters we wish to estimate/approximate. And this is almost certainly still true if you test 3, 4, or 10 different models. From this perspective though, 400+ models though provides many, many estimates of the target probability distribution, and now the central tendency of this set of estimates \-– what’s happening overall across the models — is (to my thinking) a defensible estimate of the target underlying probability distribution, and thus, a defensible test of Surprisal theory. A related perspective might instead invoke ‘multiverse’ analysis, which is the idea that summarizing the outcome of an analysis across different plausible choice points in your analysis pipeline (here, different language models) is better than taking any one of these choices as the definitive one. And post-hoc, this perspective seems largely compatible with the results in our paper \- mostly all models succeeded and failed in the same cases in capturing the human data.

I don’t think our approach yields the *definitive once and for all* test of Surprisal theory. There are tricky questions that remain, such as *what would have happened if there were exactly one model out of 400+ models that exactly fit the human data*? *Would this analogy work if the language model probabilities systematically yielded biased estimates of the ‘true’ underlying probability distribution*? But I do think that it is a conceptually coherent test of Surprisal theory, even though at its core it rests on lower-case-s surprisal estimates from a large, heterogenous set of language models that do not directly implement (some version of) Surprisal theory.[^7] By my lights the burden of evidence has been shifted: many flawed but reasonable approximations of word-level surprisal all come up short in explaining the garden path effect in regression-based eye-tracking measures, so it remains to be shown that Surprisal theory can explain syntactic disambiguation effects in comprehension.[^8]

[^1]:  “Mostly” – it has long been acknowledged that not \*all\* of incremental processing difficulty can be reduced to surprisal in the classical sense (Levy, 2008). All that matters for present purposes is that a *great deal* of these effects are thought to be reducible to surprisal, and importantly, the ones like syntactic disambiguation costs that were otherwise construed as evidence for the operation of a bespoke sentence parser (Frazier, 1979). 

[^2]:  Other prominent process level theories include Hale (2001), a related proposal that links surprisal to the total effort involved in disconfirming a projected rule under a top-down Early parser; Hale (2014) who proposes a process model based in Newell’s *Chunk Theory of Learning*; and Hoover et al. (2024) who propose a process model based on iterative sampling to find a compatible parse.  

[^3]:  I follow Buxo-Lugo et al. (2026) in using capital-S Surprisal to refer to the theory, and lower-case-s surprisal to refer to the negative log probability of an item in its context.

[^4]:  Disclaimer: I think it is ultimately wrong in key details – see Timkey et al., 2026 – but that doesn’t mean it’s not a great idea\!

[^5]:  Thanks to Adrian Staub for this characterization. 

[^6]:  Lower-case-s surprisal theory might be something like: There is some language model that predicts human processing difficulty.

[^7]:  Useful endnote: Will Timkey recently complemented this ‘broad scale’ approach with  a compelling *process-level* test of the same claims in our 2026 paper, zooming in on surprisal estimates from a language model that implements a defensible process-level claim, an analysis which yields the same results. 

[^8]:   I don’t know if they would agree with me in these details, but my perspective here has been deeply influenced by extensive discussions on this topic with Suhas Arehalli, Kuan-Jung Huang, Tal Linzen, Byung-Doh Oh, Grusha Prasad, and Will Timkey.
